I left the cinema with a sense of dissatisfaction. I think the subject matter itself could be interesting, but to spend the entire film exploring it only at a very superficial level is frustrating. It seems I'm going to need to make my own food for thought here because the film doesn't give you much to chew on.  I didn't feel any sort of genuine quandary.  It's all "poor little parents; sad face; nasty authorities; angry face".  

It avoids being completely partisan, but it also avoids asking any really difficult questions, and it completely avoids questioning itself throughout.  

The bleak landscape and settings are nice and everything.  The bleak atmosphere, the sad faces, that's really all I got from this film.  The camera is very passive.  You are pretty much just observing proceedings; if only the proceedings were actually interesting...

I will say I appreciate the film eschewing the most egregious of manipulative tropes such as tear-jerking music and the like. 

In conclusion, the film acts like a serious, sombre inquiry into what could be a very challenging subject.  It's heavy on the bleak, sad faces, and light on the substantial exploration of the subject.  No food for thought; very dissatisfying.

I think the fact that I’m not all that well-versed with Shakespeare, and Hamlet in particular, means there’s an aspect of this film that I’m unable to appreciate fully. I did study Hamlet at school, and I’ve seen it on stage too, but some decades later I feel none of that has stuck with me.

I probably don’t need to say it, everyone has said it already, but the performances throughout are absolutely flawless.

In any case, there are other aspects of this film that left me feeling underwhelmed upon exiting the cinema yesterday. 

The characters and their relationships were largely reduced to expository bullet points, and so I didn’t feel any connection to them.  Long periods of time could pass by with each scene, and you'd just be given some snippet of relationship building to work with for that whole period.  There was no food for thought there for me, it was all explained in a superficial way.

This lack of connection with the characters meant the emotional cues throughout felt all too obvious, and they didn't resonate with me.  I wasn't feeling these things alongside the characters, just being told when to feel them.

The cinematography had some nice compositions. I think maybe it’s apt that they were largely static scenes, such as you’d see on stage. I really enjoyed the cinematographer’s work in Cold War. Every shot in that film felt like art. I didn’t feel that way here.

I felt more genuine emotion seeing the video of the cast dancing in the theatre at the end of production than I did in the film’s final scene proper, whose culmination I thought was bizarre and quite unconvincing!

If it gets a physical release with a longer cut allowing it to breathe more, I’ll give it another go.

Second watch. An absolute pleasure to behold from start to end.

This is an incredible looking film: The angles, framing, composition, lighting, contrast, camera movement. More than that though, it's the storytelling that's brilliant, and that's the magic. It's all very well having every frame be a painting, but this isn't a painting, it's a living breathing story and everything is working together in perfect unison to tell that story.

A slightly ridiculous example, but the infamous "crotch shot" of Inspector Lohmann. The investigation is going nowhere. Watched in a 4DX cinema, in 3D, with a French audio track!  Not normally what I'd choose, but it's what was available!

The 4DX thing, with the chairs shaking around and water spraying, wind, and smoke machines and stuff; well it's a total gimmick, and the chairs in the place do not suit someone who's 6'2"; I think they're made for kids or miniature people. Anyway, it's not what I'd have chosen, but it was my chance of seeing T2 on a big screen here, so I wasn't going to turn down the opportunity!

The 3D.  Again, I'd rather see it without the 3D, but at points it did look really nice, mainly just in scenes with nice basic composition rather than the frenetic action scenes, to my mind.

I have the film on 4k, and this 2017 restoration has been a little controversial.  I think it works OK with 3D.  Having the absolute visual fidelity somewhat compromised by 3D and the 4DX nonsense throwing you around distracts from the overdone DNR, and I actually thought it was _really_ nice looking in a lot of places.

I don't want to sound negative; this is an incredible film, and I _really_ enjoyed seeing it a lot tonight.  It maybe represents the best of a golden era of physical effects and stunts, but it also hails the ushering in of a new era, with the CGI, but before films became just disconnected from reality; people with ping-pong balls on their elbows and knees pretending to be somewhere while in a green-screen room.  

Overall, I'm really glad I got to see T2 on a big screen.  Hopefully we'll get a good restoration of this film one day, and I'd like to see it on a big screen with a comfortable seat that doesn't move around and spray me with stuff, and without 3D.

I'm giving it 4.9 stars, because T1 will always be my favourite, and because of the questionable choices made in the restoration.

Powell riding across the landscape in silouhette.

Just so many great, memorable scenes!

The more I think about the film, the more I love it!
